questions.stem: The Indian economy is best described as a:

options.explanation: Correct. India has lower average income and a large farm-dependent workforce (developing), and private and public sectors coexist (mixed).
India's average income, capital stock and human-development indicators are still those of a developing economy, and it is not purely capitalist.
India has a large private sector alongside the public sector, so it is not a fully centrally planned economy.
India has large modern industrial and services sectors, so it is far more than a subsistence economy.

questions.sourceRef: India as a developing (emerging) mixed economy

questions.stem: In calling India a 'mixed economy', the word 'mixed' refers to the coexistence of:

options.explanation: Every economy has both agriculture and industry; that mix is not what defines a mixed economy.
Urban and rural areas exist in all economies; this is not the meaning of a mixed economy.
Correct. A mixed economy is one in which private enterprise and the public (state) sector operate side by side.
The presence of foreign firms is about openness, not the private-public mix that defines a mixed economy.

questions.sourceRef: Mixed economy = private and public sectors coexist

questions.stem: Which of the following is a typical feature of a developing economy?

options.text: Most of the workforce is employed in high-technology services
options.explanation: A large high-technology services workforce is a mark of a developed economy, not a developing one.

options.text: A large share of the population depends on agriculture, with relatively low income and capital
options.explanation: Correct. Lower average income, scarce capital and heavy dependence on agriculture are classic features of a developing economy.

options.text: A very high average income and abundant capital
options.explanation: High average income and abundant capital describe a developed economy.

options.text: The complete absence of any modern industry
options.explanation: Developing economies do have modern industry; it simply coexists with a large traditional sector.

questions.sourceRef: Features of a developing economy

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Overview · What India is not
questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Indian economy is FALSE?

options.explanation: True — the private and public sectors coexist in India.
True — India is classed as a developing or emerging economy.

options.text: It has a large services sector
options.explanation: True — services form the largest part of India's output.
Correct. This is the false statement: India is a developing, not a developed, economy.

questions.sourceRef: India is developing, not developed

questions.stem: Economic dualism in the Indian economy means the coexistence of:

options.explanation: Dualism is an economic feature, not a political arrangement.

options.text: a modern sector and a traditional sector side by side
options.explanation: Correct. Dualism is the coexistence of a modern, organised sector with a traditional, subsistence sector — a mark of a developing economy.
Exports and imports describe trade, not the modern-traditional split that dualism names.
Two levels of government is federalism, not economic dualism.

readLink.label: Read: Features of the Indian economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Dualism = modern and traditional sectors coexist

questions.stem: Which statement best captures agriculture's place in the Indian economy over time?

options.text: Its share of both output and employment has risen
options.explanation: Agriculture's share of output has fallen over time, not risen.

options.text: It employs almost no one and produces almost nothing
options.explanation: Agriculture still supports a very large share of the workforce and remains vital for food and raw materials.

options.text: It still employs a large share of the workforce, though its share of output has fallen
options.explanation: Correct. A big workforce share with a smaller output share is the characteristic pattern, pointing to relatively low productivity.

options.text: Its share of output is larger than that of services
options.explanation: Services, not agriculture, form the largest share of output.

readLink.label: Read: Features of the Indian economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Agriculture: large workforce share, smaller output share

questions.stem: A large share of people of working age in the population is described as a 'demographic dividend' when it:

options.explanation: Correct. A young, large working-age population is a dividend when it is put to productive work, and a burden when it cannot find work.
An unemployed young workforce is a burden, not a dividend; the dividend depends on productive employment.
A demographic dividend comes from a large working-age share, not from a large retired population.
A shrinking working-age population would remove the dividend, not create it.

readLink.label: Read: Features of the Indian economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Demographic dividend depends on productive employment of the young workforce

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Features · Largest sector by output
questions.stem: In terms of share of total output, the largest sector of the Indian economy is the:

options.explanation: The primary sector's share of output has fallen over time and is no longer the largest.
Industry's share of output is significant but not the largest of the three.
Public versus private is a question of ownership, not one of the three output sectors being asked about.
Correct. Services form the largest share of India's output, a defining structural feature.

readLink.label: Read: Features of the Indian economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Services are the largest share of output

questions.stem: The 'informal' or 'unorganised' sector of the Indian economy is characterised by:

options.text: large registered firms with formal contracts
options.explanation: Large registered firms with formal contracts belong to the organised sector, the opposite of the informal sector.

options.text: small, largely unregistered units and casual work without formal contracts or social security
options.explanation: Correct. The informal sector is made up of small unregistered units, self-employment and casual labour outside formal regulation and benefits.
Government-owned enterprises are part of the organised public sector, not the informal sector.
Foreign multinationals are organised, formal firms, not informal-sector units.

readLink.label: Read: Features of the Indian economy, §2 →

questions.sourceRef: Informal sector = small unregistered units, casual work, no formal contracts

questions.stem: Which of the following is an activity of the primary sector?

options.explanation: Correct. Fishing draws a good directly from nature, so it belongs to the primary sector.
Manufacturing transforms raw materials into goods, so it is a secondary-sector activity.
Banking provides a service, so it belongs to the tertiary sector.
A call centre provides a service, so it is a tertiary-sector activity.

questions.sourceRef: Primary sector draws goods directly from nature

questions.stem: The secondary sector of an economy is also called the:

options.explanation: The agricultural sector is the primary sector, not the secondary.
The services sector is the tertiary sector, not the secondary.
Correct. The secondary sector transforms raw materials into goods and is also called the manufacturing or industrial sector.
The public sector is defined by government ownership, not by being one of the three output sectors.

questions.sourceRef: Secondary sector = manufacturing / industry

questions.stem: Which of the following belongs to the tertiary sector?

options.explanation: Growing wheat draws a good from nature, so it is a primary-sector activity.
Correct. Transport and banking provide services rather than goods, so they belong to the tertiary (services) sector.
Weaving cloth transforms raw material into a good, so it is a secondary-sector activity.
Quarrying takes stone directly from the earth, so it is a primary-sector activity.

questions.sourceRef: Tertiary sector = services (transport, banking, trade)

questions.stem: Mining and quarrying are classified under the:

options.text: secondary sector, because they feel industrial
options.explanation: Although mining feels industrial, it does not transform raw materials; it extracts them, so it is not secondary.

options.text: tertiary sector, because they need machinery
options.explanation: Needing machinery does not make an activity a service; mining produces a raw material, not a service.

options.text: public sector, because minerals are state-owned
options.explanation: Ownership does not decide the output sector; mining is classified by what it does — extracting from nature.

options.text: primary sector, because they take goods directly from nature
options.explanation: Correct. Mining draws minerals directly from the earth, so it is a primary-sector activity despite feeling industrial.

questions.sourceRef: Mining is a primary-sector activity

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Three sectors · Classifying a service
questions.stem: A software company writing programs for overseas clients belongs to the:

options.explanation: The primary sector draws goods from nature; writing software does neither.
The secondary sector transforms raw materials into goods; software is a service, not a manufactured good.
Correct. Software is a knowledge-based service, so it belongs to the tertiary sector (sometimes carved out as a 'quaternary' sub-group).
A software company can be a large, organised firm; software is a tertiary-sector activity regardless of formality.

questions.sourceRef: Software / IT is a tertiary-sector service

questions.stem: Construction of buildings and roads is generally classified under the:

options.explanation: Correct. Construction transforms materials into finished physical structures, so it is grouped with the secondary (industrial) sector.
Construction does not draw goods directly from nature; it uses processed materials, so it is not primary.
Construction produces physical structures rather than pure services, so it is treated as secondary, not tertiary.

options.text: no sector, as it produces nothing
options.explanation: Construction clearly produces buildings and infrastructure; it is a secondary-sector activity.

questions.sourceRef: Construction is a secondary-sector activity

questions.stem: Which sector-and-example pairing is correct?

options.explanation: A textile mill transforms cotton into cloth, so it is secondary, not primary.
Correct. A car assembly plant transforms parts into finished cars, a secondary-sector (manufacturing) activity.
Dairy farming is an allied agricultural activity, so it is primary, not tertiary.
A retail shop provides a trading service, so it is tertiary, not primary.

questions.sourceRef: Correct sector-example pairings

questions.stem: As an economy develops, the centre of gravity of output typically shifts in the direction:

options.explanation: This reverses the usual pattern; development moves weight toward services, not back to agriculture.
The usual pattern begins with the primary sector, not the secondary.
This is not the recognised sequence; the shift starts from the primary sector.
Correct. Weight moves from agriculture to industry and then to services as an economy matures.

questions.sourceRef: Structural shift runs primary → secondary → tertiary

questions.stem: A notable feature of India's structural change is that:

options.text: the services sector has grown fastest and become the largest part of output
options.explanation: Correct. India is often described as having a services-led structure, with the tertiary sector the largest contributor to output.

options.text: the primary sector's share of output has kept rising
options.explanation: The primary sector's share of output has fallen over time, not risen.

options.text: the secondary sector now produces almost all output
options.explanation: Industry is important but does not produce almost all output; services are the largest.

options.text: all three sectors have exactly equal shares
options.explanation: The three sectors do not have equal shares; services are the largest.

questions.sourceRef: India's services-led structural change

questions.stem: Over the decades since independence, the share of the primary sector in India's output has:

options.explanation: The primary sector's output share has fallen, not risen, as the economy has developed.
The share has changed markedly over time; it has not stayed constant.

options.text: become larger than the services sector's share
options.explanation: Services now form a larger share of output than the primary sector.

options.text: fallen steadily, even though it still employs a large workforce
options.explanation: Correct. The primary sector's output share has declined over time while it still employs a large share of the workforce.

questions.sourceRef: Falling primary output share with a still-large workforce

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Structural shift · Labour productivity gap
questions.stem: Because the workforce has moved between sectors more slowly than output has, a disproportionate share of workers remains in agriculture. This is a reason why policy stresses:

options.text: reducing the total population by any means
options.explanation: The concern is productivity and the movement of surplus labour, not simply reducing population.

options.text: raising farm productivity and moving surplus farm labour into industry and services
options.explanation: Correct. With too many workers left in low-productivity agriculture, policy stresses raising productivity and shifting surplus labour to other sectors.
Closing industry and services would worsen the problem, not solve it; the aim is to absorb surplus farm labour into them.
Restricting movement out of agriculture would trap surplus labour in low-productivity work, the opposite of the aim.

questions.sourceRef: Surplus low-productivity farm labour and the policy response

questions.stem: The four conventional objectives of economic planning in India are:

options.explanation: Correct. These four — a bigger economy, a fairer share, less external dependence, and upgraded technology and structure — are the standard objectives of Indian planning.
Inflation, deflation and taxation are outcomes or instruments, not the stated objectives of planning.
These describe market outcomes and reform strands, not the four objectives of planning.
War, expansion and conquest are not objectives of economic planning.

questions.sourceRef: Objectives of planning: growth, equity, self-reliance, modernization

questions.stem: As an objective of Indian planning, 'self-reliance' means:

options.text: producing only luxury goods for export
options.explanation: Self-reliance is about reducing dependence on foreign aid and imports, not about specialising in luxury exports.
Maximising imports is the opposite of self-reliance, which seeks to reduce dependence on imports.

options.text: reducing dependence on foreign aid and imports by building the country's own productive capacity
options.explanation: Correct. Self-reliance means building domestic capacity, especially in key industries, so the country depends less on foreign aid and imports.

options.text: ending all trade with other countries
options.explanation: Self-reliance does not require ending all trade; it means reducing dependence, not autarky.

questions.sourceRef: Self-reliance = reducing dependence on foreign aid and imports

questions.stem: Which of the following was NOT a stated objective of economic planning in India?

options.explanation: Growth is one of the four stated objectives of planning.
Equity (reducing inequality) is one of the four stated objectives of planning.
Modernization is one of the four stated objectives of planning.

options.text: Maximising the private profit of individual firms
options.explanation: Correct. Maximising individual firms' private profit is not an objective of national planning, which aims at growth, equity, self-reliance and modernization.

questions.sourceRef: Private profit maximisation is not a planning objective

questions.stem: A Five-Year Plan in India was:

options.text: a private company's five-year sales target
options.explanation: A Five-Year Plan was a national planning document, not a single company's sales target.

options.text: a document setting the economy's goals, sectors to develop and public investment for a five-year block
options.explanation: Correct. Each Five-Year Plan laid out national goals, the sectors to be developed and the public investment to be made over five years.

options.text: a five-year ban on all imports
options.explanation: A Five-Year Plan was a development plan, not an import ban.

options.text: a five-year fixed interest rate set by banks
options.explanation: A Five-Year Plan had nothing to do with fixing bank interest rates.

questions.sourceRef: Five-Year Plan = five-year document of goals and public investment

questions.stem: The planning objective of 'equity' (social justice) is chiefly concerned with:

options.text: increasing the total size of national output only
options.explanation: Increasing total output is the objective of growth; equity is about how output is shared, not its size.
Raising technology is the objective of modernization, not equity.

options.text: reducing poverty and the inequalities of income and wealth
options.explanation: Correct. Equity aims to reduce poverty and income and wealth inequality so that growth reaches weaker sections.

options.text: cutting all links with the world economy
options.explanation: Cutting links with the world relates loosely to self-reliance, not to equity, which is about fair distribution.

questions.sourceRef: Equity = reducing poverty and income/wealth inequality

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Planning bodies · NITI Aayog full form
questions.stem: NITI Aayog stands for the:

options.explanation: Correct. NITI Aayog is the National Institution for Transforming India, the body that replaced the Planning Commission.

options.text: National Investment and Trade Institute of India
options.explanation: This is not the meaning of the acronym; NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India.
This is not the meaning of the acronym; NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India.
This is not the meaning of the acronym; NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India.

readLink.label: Read: Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: NITI Aayog = National Institution for Transforming India

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Planning bodies · Year of change
questions.stem: In which year did NITI Aayog replace the Planning Commission?

options.explanation: 1991 is the year of the LPG economic reforms, not the year NITI Aayog was created.
Correct. NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
The First Five-Year Plan era began around this time; NITI Aayog came much later, in 2015.
NITI Aayog was created in 2015, not 2000.

readLink.label: Read: Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Planning Commission replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Planning bodies · Nature of NITI Aayog
questions.stem: NITI Aayog is best described as:

options.text: a resource-allocating body that prepares numbered Five-Year Plans
options.explanation: Allocating resources and preparing Five-Year Plans describes the old Planning Commission, not NITI Aayog.

options.text: a commercial bank owned by the government
options.explanation: NITI Aayog is a policy body, not a bank.

options.text: a policy think-tank and advisory body
options.explanation: Correct. NITI Aayog is designed as a policy think-tank that advises the government and designs long-term strategy.

options.text: a court that settles economic disputes
options.explanation: NITI Aayog is an advisory policy body, not a court.

readLink.label: Read: Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: NITI Aayog = policy think-tank and advisory body

questions.stem: A key idea associated with NITI Aayog is 'cooperative federalism', which means:

options.text: handing plans down to the states from the centre
options.explanation: Handing plans down from the centre is the old top-down style of the Planning Commission, not cooperative federalism.
Cooperative federalism works with the states; it does not abolish them.

options.text: letting only the central government make every decision
options.explanation: Centralising all decisions is the opposite of cooperative federalism, which shares the effort with the states.

options.text: working with the states as partners rather than dictating to them
options.explanation: Correct. Cooperative federalism means the centre works with the states as partners, a shift from the old top-down approach to a more bottom-up one.

readLink.label: Read: Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Cooperative federalism = centre works with states as partners

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Planning bodies · Commission vs NITI Aayog
questions.stem: Which statement correctly contrasts the Planning Commission with NITI Aayog?

options.text: The Planning Commission allocated resources and planned top-down; NITI Aayog is a think-tank built on cooperative federalism
options.explanation: Correct. The old Commission was a resource-allocating, top-down planner, while NITI Aayog is an advisory think-tank working with the states.

options.text: Both bodies allocate resources and prepare Five-Year Plans in exactly the same way
options.explanation: They differ: NITI Aayog does not allocate resources or prepare numbered Five-Year Plans as the Commission did.

options.text: NITI Aayog is older than the Planning Commission
options.explanation: The Planning Commission is the older body; NITI Aayog replaced it in 2015.

options.text: The Planning Commission was a think-tank; NITI Aayog allocates all resources
options.explanation: This reverses the two: the Commission allocated resources, and NITI Aayog is the think-tank.

readLink.label: Read: Planning Commission to NITI Aayog, §6 →

questions.sourceRef: Contrast: Commission (top-down, resource-allocating) vs NITI Aayog (think-tank, cooperative federalism)

questions.stem: The 1991 economic reforms in India were triggered by a severe:

options.explanation: The trigger was an external payments crisis, not a banking merger.
Correct. Foreign-exchange reserves fell so low that India could barely pay for a few weeks of imports, forcing the reforms.
A boom is not a crisis; the reforms followed a foreign-exchange crisis, not a boom.

options.text: fall in the general price level (deflation)
options.explanation: The crisis was in external payments and reserves, not a general fall in prices.

questions.sourceRef: 1991 reforms triggered by a balance-of-payments crisis

questions.stem: In the context of the 1991 reforms, 'LPG' stands for:

options.explanation: This is not the meaning of LPG in the reforms context.
This is not the meaning of LPG in the reforms context.
Correct. The 1991 reform package is summarised as Liberalization, Privatization and Globalization.
These describe the pre-reform controlled economy, the opposite of what the LPG reforms did.

questions.sourceRef: LPG = Liberalization, Privatization, Globalization

questions.stem: Abolishing the industrial licensing requirement for most industries (delicensing) is an example of:

options.explanation: Correct. Removing internal controls such as industrial licensing frees domestic business, which is the essence of liberalization.
Privatization is about shifting ownership from the state to private hands, not about removing licensing.
Globalization is about opening to world trade and foreign investment, not about domestic delicensing.
Nationalization means taking firms into state ownership, the opposite direction from the 1991 reforms.

questions.sourceRef: Delicensing = Liberalization

questions.stem: Selling part of the government's shareholding in a public-sector undertaking (disinvestment) is an example of:

options.explanation: Liberalization removes internal controls such as licensing; disinvestment is about changing ownership.
Globalization opens the economy to world trade and investment; disinvestment is a domestic ownership change.
Nationalization increases state ownership; disinvestment reduces it, so it is the opposite.
Correct. Disinvestment reduces the state's ownership stake and widens the private sector's role, which is privatization.

questions.sourceRef: Disinvestment = Privatization

questions.stem: Cutting import tariffs and opening the economy to foreign investment is an example of:

options.explanation: Removing internal controls is liberalization, but cutting import tariffs and opening to foreign investment specifically links the economy to the world — globalization.
Correct. Reducing trade barriers and opening to foreign investment integrates India with the world economy, which is globalization.
Privatization is about ownership moving from state to private hands, not about opening to trade.
Central planning is the controlled model the reforms moved away from, not the opening to trade.

questions.sourceRef: Opening to trade and foreign investment = Globalization

questions.stem: Before 1991, the requirement that private firms obtain a government licence to set up or expand was popularly called the:

options.explanation: The Green Revolution refers to the rise in farm output from new seeds and techniques, not to industrial licensing.
The White Revolution refers to the growth of milk production, not to industrial licensing.
Correct. The system of compulsory industrial licences before 1991 was popularly called the 'Licence Raj'.
Consumer sovereignty is a feature of a market economy, not a name for the licensing system.

questions.sourceRef: Pre-1991 industrial licensing = 'Licence Raj'

questions.topic: Ch 10 · 1991 reforms · Sorting P from G
questions.stem: Two measures are proposed: (i) reducing the government's stake in a state-owned steel firm, and (ii) allowing foreign direct investment into a new industry. These illustrate, respectively:

options.explanation: Correct. Reducing the state's stake is privatization; allowing foreign direct investment opens the economy outward, which is globalization.
This reverses the pairing: reducing the state's stake is privatization, and foreign investment is globalization, not the other way round.
Neither measure is delicensing of domestic controls; (i) is privatization and (ii) is globalization.
Reducing a state stake is the opposite of nationalization, and opening to foreign investment is globalization, not liberalization.

questions.sourceRef: Disinvestment = P; foreign investment = G

questions.stem: The 'poverty line' is:

options.text: the average income of the whole population
options.explanation: The poverty line is a minimum threshold, not the average income of the population.

options.text: a threshold level of consumption or income below which a person is counted as poor
options.explanation: Correct. The poverty line is the minimum consumption or income level; those below it are counted as poor.

options.text: the highest income earned in the economy
options.explanation: The poverty line marks a minimum, not the highest income.

options.text: the total value of a country's output
options.explanation: Total output is national income, not the poverty line.

questions.sourceRef: Poverty line = minimum consumption/income threshold

questions.stem: The 'head-count ratio' of poverty measures:

options.text: the average amount by which the poor fall below the poverty line
options.explanation: The gap below the line is captured by other measures (such as the poverty gap), not by the head-count ratio.

options.text: the total money value of goods the poor consume
options.explanation: The head-count ratio counts people, not the money value of their consumption.

options.text: the highest income in the poorest region
options.explanation: The head-count ratio is a proportion of people below the line, not a top income figure.

options.text: the proportion of the population below the poverty line
options.explanation: Correct. The head-count ratio is simply the share of the population that falls below the poverty line.

questions.sourceRef: Head-count ratio = proportion of population below the poverty line

questions.stem: The difference between absolute and relative poverty is that:

options.text: absolute poverty compares people with others, while relative poverty uses a fixed minimum
options.explanation: This reverses the two: absolute poverty uses a fixed minimum, and relative poverty compares people with others.

options.text: both mean exactly the same thing
options.explanation: They are distinct ideas: one uses a fixed standard, the other compares people within a society.

options.text: relative poverty can never exist in a rich country
options.explanation: Relative poverty compares people with others, so it can exist even in rich countries where some are far below the rest.

options.text: absolute poverty is measured against a fixed minimum, while relative poverty compares people with others in society
options.explanation: Correct. Absolute poverty uses a fixed poverty line; relative poverty compares people with others, so it really measures inequality.

questions.sourceRef: Absolute (fixed minimum) vs relative (compared with others) poverty

questions.stem: In the economic sense, a person is 'unemployed' when they are:

options.text: willing and able to work at the going wage but cannot find work
options.explanation: Correct. Unemployment means being willing and able to work at the going wage yet unable to find a job.

options.text: unwilling to work at any wage
options.explanation: Someone unwilling to work is not counted as unemployed; unemployment requires willingness to work.

options.text: too old or too ill to work
options.explanation: A person unable to work is outside the labour force, not counted as unemployed.
A person already in full-time work is employed, not unemployed.

questions.sourceRef: Unemployment = willing and able to work at the going wage but no job

questions.stem: Where more people work on a task than are really needed, so that some contribute little or nothing to output, the unemployment is called:

options.explanation: Frictional unemployment is short-term joblessness while moving between jobs, not surplus workers on one task.
Cyclical unemployment rises in a downturn; it is not about too many workers on a single task.
Correct. Disguised unemployment is where surplus workers add little or nothing to output — their marginal productivity is near zero, common in agriculture.
Seasonal unemployment is idleness in the off-season, not surplus workers during the working period.

questions.sourceRef: Disguised unemployment = surplus workers, near-zero marginal productivity

questions.stem: A farm labourer who has no work between the sowing and harvest seasons is an example of:

options.explanation: Structural unemployment comes from a skills or location mismatch, not from the off-season of an activity.
Correct. Work exists only in certain seasons and the labourer is idle in between, which is seasonal unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment is tied to the business cycle (a downturn), not to the farming calendar.
Disguised unemployment is surplus workers adding nothing during work; this case is about idleness in the off-season.

questions.sourceRef: Seasonal unemployment = idle in the off-season

questions.stem: When workers lose their jobs because their skills no longer match the jobs available as the economy's structure changes, the unemployment is called:

options.explanation: Seasonal unemployment is tied to the off-season of an activity, not to a skills mismatch.
Frictional unemployment is short-term joblessness between jobs, not a lasting skills mismatch.
Cyclical unemployment follows the business cycle; this case is about a structural mismatch of skills.
Correct. Joblessness from a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the available jobs is structural unemployment.

questions.sourceRef: Structural unemployment = skills/location mismatch

questions.stem: Workers are laid off across many firms during a general economic slump. A graduate, separately, spends a few weeks searching between quitting one job and starting the next. These two cases are, respectively:

options.explanation: Correct. Widespread lay-offs in a slump are cyclical unemployment; a short search between jobs is frictional unemployment.
This reverses the two: the slump case is cyclical and the short job search is frictional, not the other way round.
Neither case fits: a slump is cyclical, not structural, and a short search is frictional, not seasonal.
Neither case fits: the slump is cyclical, not disguised, and the job search is frictional, not structural.

questions.sourceRef: Slump lay-offs = cyclical; short job search = frictional

questions.stem: Inflation is best defined as:

options.text: a one-off rise in the price of a single good
options.explanation: Inflation is a general, sustained rise, not a one-off change in one good's price.

options.text: a sustained rise in the general level of prices
options.explanation: Correct. Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, which erodes the purchasing power of money.

options.text: an increase in the quantity of goods produced
options.explanation: A rise in output is growth, not inflation; inflation concerns the general price level.

options.text: a fall in the general level of prices
options.explanation: A sustained fall in the general price level is deflation, the opposite of inflation.

questions.sourceRef: Inflation = sustained rise in the general price level

questions.stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines which three dimensions?

options.explanation: These are measures of openness and trade, not the dimensions of the HDI.

options.text: Inflation, unemployment and the budget deficit
options.explanation: These are macroeconomic indicators, not the components of the HDI.

options.text: A long and healthy life, knowledge (education), and a decent standard of living (income)
options.explanation: Correct. The HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (knowledge) and income (standard of living).
These describe a country's size and endowment, not the HDI's three dimensions.

questions.sourceRef: HDI = health + education + income

questions.stem: In development economics, 'infrastructure' refers chiefly to:

options.text: the stock of luxury consumer goods held by households
options.explanation: Luxury consumer goods are not infrastructure; infrastructure is the basic facilities that support the whole economy.

options.text: the profits earned by private firms
options.explanation: Profits are a financial result, not infrastructure.

options.text: the total money supply in the economy
options.explanation: The money supply is a monetary quantity, not the physical and institutional facilities that infrastructure names.

options.text: the basic physical and institutional facilities such as power, transport, communication and finance
options.explanation: Correct. Infrastructure is the basic facilities — power, roads, railways, ports, water, telecom and financial and educational services — on which the rest of the economy rests.

questions.sourceRef: Infrastructure = basic physical and institutional facilities

questions.topic: Ch 10 · Sector roles · Role of industry
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the role of the industrial (secondary) sector in growth?

options.text: It raises productivity, creates productive jobs, produces capital goods, and reduces import dependence
options.explanation: Correct. Industry is the classic engine of modernisation — raising productivity, creating better jobs, producing capital goods and cutting import dependence.

options.text: It only provides services such as banking and transport
options.explanation: Providing services is the role of the tertiary sector, not industry.

options.text: It draws raw materials directly from nature
options.explanation: Drawing raw materials from nature is the role of the primary sector, not industry.

options.text: It plays no part in employment or growth
options.explanation: Industry is a major source of productive employment and growth, so this is incorrect.

questions.sourceRef: Industry: modernisation, capital goods, productive jobs, less import dependence

questions.topic: Ch 10 · World economy · Openness and FDI
questions.stem: Since 1991, India's integration with the world economy is shown by, among other things:

options.text: a rise in import tariffs and a ban on foreign investment
options.explanation: Integration involved cutting import tariffs and welcoming foreign investment, not raising barriers and banning it.
India takes part in bodies such as the WTO; integration meant engaging with, not withdrawing from, international institutions.

options.text: lower import tariffs, more foreign direct investment, and membership of the WTO
options.explanation: Correct. Openness rose through lower trade barriers, inflows of foreign direct and portfolio investment, and participation in the WTO.

options.text: becoming a fully closed, inward-looking economy
options.explanation: India moved from a relatively closed economy toward an open one, the opposite of becoming fully closed.

readLink.label: Read: India and the world economy, §12 →

questions.sourceRef: Post-1991 openness: lower tariffs, FDI, WTO membership
